parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Two coils are wound on an iron bar, as shown in Fig. 7.1.

[[fig:f1]]

Coil 1 is connected to a potential difference (p.d.) *V*₁ that gives rise to a magnetic field in the iron bar.

Fig. 7.2 shows the variation with time *t* of the magnetic flux density *B* in the iron bar.

[[fig:f2]]

A voltmeter measures the electromotive force (e.m.f.) *V*₂ that is induced across coil 2.

On Fig. 7.3, sketch the variation with *t* of *V*₂ between *t* = 0 and *t* = 0.40 s.

[[fig:f3]]

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.lead:
Coil 2 in (b) is now replaced with a copper ring that rests loosely on top of coil 1. The supply to coil 1 is replaced with a cell and a switch that is initially open, as shown in Fig. 7.4.

[[fig:f4]]
parts.text:
The switch is now closed. As it is closed, the copper ring is observed to jump upwards.

Explain why this happens.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, what would be the effect of repeating the procedure in (c)(i) with the terminals of the cell reversed.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.1
figures.alt: Two coils are wound around a vertical iron bar, with coil 1 connected to a p.d. supply and coil 2 connected to a voltmeter.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.2
figures.alt: A graph of magnetic flux density B against time, rising to a positive peak, falling steeply to a negative peak, then rising back to zero.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.3
figures.alt: A blank graph grid with V₂ on the vertical axis and time t in seconds on the horizontal axis from 0 to 0.4.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.4
figures.alt: A copper ring rests on top of a coil wound around an iron bar, with the coil connected to a cell and switch.
